name: Amurdak
confidence_why: Handelsmann 1991, the only description of Amurdak that addresses stress, reports from his own fieldwork that he could not isolate a consistent stressed syllable and obtained no speaker intuitions, and Capell 1942 and Mailhammer 2014 say nothing about stress, so the record stands on one first-hand source with nothing against it.
catalog_citation: Handelsmann, Robert. 1991. Towards a description of Amurdak: a language of Northern Australia. Honours thesis, Department of Linguistics & Language Studies, University of Melbourne, submitted November 1991. vii + 116 pp. Open scan: ANU Open Research, hdl.handle.net/1885/300156.
catalog_locator: Ch. 2 Phonology, section 2.3 Stress, p. 38 (of the ANU scan)
catalog_quote: I have as yet been unable to isolate the precise combination of pitch, intensity and length which constitutes stress or prominance in Amurdak. What I occasionally perceive as a stressed syllable in one instantiation of a word, I often perceive as not stressed in another instantiation of the same word. This is common in Iwaidja. Pym & Larrimore (1979) include a chapter on 'discourse phonology' in their description of Iwaidja, devoted to the question of why word stress appeared to vary. They write: The results of the study showed that the way in which syllables were grouped together was of greater significance than than the placement of stress. Tests showed that wrong grouping of syllables produced unintelligible utterances, while variations in stress placement did not affect intelligibility to nearly the same extent (p.11) I have been unsuccessful in getting native speakers' intuitions in this area.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.citation: Handelsmann, Robert. 1991. Towards a description of Amurdak: a language of Northern Australia. Honours thesis, Department of Linguistics & Language Studies, University of Melbourne (submitted November 1991). vii + 116 pp.
new_statements.locator: §2.3 Stress, p. 38 (PDF page 47 of the ANU scan; page scan page_pins/)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (125 pp., Acrobat scanned layer; extracted text gives header "Phonology 38" and "2.3 Stress") and the page scan page_pins/. The quoted passage is on that page verbatim, including the spelling "prominance" and the closing sentence "I have been unsuccessful in getting native speakers' intuitions in this area." (garbled in the scanned text at line 1883 but clean on the page scan); the "[..]" elides only the indented Pym & Larrimore block quote, which is also present as reported. §2.3 is the whole of the thesis' stress treatment: no placement rule, no secondary stress, no stress marks in transcriptions (0 IPA stress marks in the text); the only other 'stress' hits are the Gagudju /l/ all…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand description declines to give a placement rule: the author could not identify a consistent phonetic correlate of stress, and the syllable heard as prominent shifts from one token of a word to another; he likens this to Iwaidja, where Pym & Larrimore (1979: 11) found syllable grouping mattered more for intelligibility than stress placement. No fixed, weight-based or lexical rule is stated or implied.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the section is a statement of indeterminacy rather than a rule. Elsewhere the thesis mentions speakers' slow syllabifications sometimes breaking words into 'groups of syllables' whose status (morphological or metrical) is unclear (p. 12, fn. 6), and occasional compensatory vowel lengthening before simplified clusters (§2.6, p. 45) — neither is tied to stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, elicited citation forms and repeated tokens of single words from two speakers (Big Bill Neidjie and Nelson Mulurinj), fieldwork 1990-91; no discourse-level analysis was done for Amurdak.
new_statements.identity_note: Handelsmann 1991 describes the Amurdak of two speakers, Big Bill Neidjie and Nelson Mulurinj, recorded around Oenpelli / Mt Borradaile (East Alligator area) in 1990-91; the thesis names no dialect (Wikipedia lists Urrirk and Gidjurra as dialects; glottocode amar1271 is language-level). Capell 1942 calls the language 'Amarag' (also 'Umoriu' after Spencer) — same language, single Oenpelli speaker. No differently-named variety is at issue.

sources.note: Ch. 2 Phonology has a dedicated §2.3 Stress (p. 38): the author could not isolate the combination of pitch, intensity and length that constitutes stress in Amurdak; a syllable perceived as stressed in one token of a word is perceived as unstressed in another token of the same word ('This is common in Iwaidja', citing Pym & Larrimore 1979 discourse phonology, p. 11); no native-speaker intuitions obtained. No placement rule given anywhere in the thesis (only other 'stress' hits are a quotation about Gagudju /l/ allophony, p. 10, and bibliography entries).
Consonant and vowel tables attributed to Mailhammer 2009 and Evans 1998; nothing on stress. Lists Handelsmann 1991, Mailhammer 2009, Neidjie et al. 2009 Amurdak inyman, Evans 1998.
